title: How One Bakery Burned Down London
sources: London Museum, 'The Great Fire of London' (began 2 September 1666 in Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane; burned for four days; about 13,200 houses, 87 parish churches and St Paul's Cathedral destroyed)
Royal Museums Greenwich, 'The Great Fire of London' (wooden houses, strong east wind, the Lord Mayor's dismissive response, houses blown up to create firebreaks)
Rebuilding Act 1667: new buildings in brick and stone

lines.text: In sixteen sixty-six, a tiny bakery fire burned down most of London.
lines.caps: In *1666, | a tiny *bakery fire | burned down *London.

lines.text: It started just after midnight, in Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane.
lines.caps: Just after *midnight, | in Farriner's *bakery | on Pudding *Lane.

lines.text: London was packed with wooden houses, and a strong wind was blowing,
so the flames jumped from roof to roof.
The Lord Mayor was woken up, but he shrugged it off.
For four days, the city burned.
Thirteen thousand houses, eighty-seven churches, and St Paul's Cathedral were gone.
lines.caps: *13,000 houses, | *87 churches, | and St Paul's | were *gone.

lines.text: In the end, they blew up whole streets to stop it spreading.
And when London was rebuilt, it was built in brick and stone.
All because of one small bakery.
